correctness.rationale: Definitions and quantifiers specify m>=n>=2, sigma>0 and predictable perpendicular signals of fixed lengths. Conditional Gaussian splitting yields central/noncentral chi-square inverse moments for exponents below codimension; the append-column inequality inductively bounds history moments. A first-order Gram-nullspace eigenvalue calculation gives the true singular coefficient D. Uniform-in-direction small-ball asymptotics and explicit integrable domination justify exchange of limits, giving the finite positive gamma coefficient; the positive asymptotic and finite-moment bound prove iff p<d. The standalone script passed 300 direct singular-limit tests, 255 smallest-singular-value tests, two exact baseline laws, and four noncentral-F quadratures. Finite checks support but do not replace proof.

originality.rationale: The exact conditional singular-column coefficient, domination through integrability of the preceding nonlinear adaptive column history, and resulting sharp full-condition-number tail constant are absent from the examined primary QR source, whose claims stop at noncentral-F residual laws and product upper bounds. The iid Gaussian/Wishart tail literature obtains analogous codimension exponents for a different ensemble and does not imply the constant for predictable normalized columns. Actual semantic searches and previous claims were checked; residual unindexed-equivalence risk remains.

value.rationale: In the 2024 Gaussian-noise QR orthogonalization model, published multi-step guarantees describe high-probability conditioning but do not say whether expected conditioning exists or how extreme events scale. The theorem gives a sharp codimension-dependent moment transition, a true (rather than certified-upper-bound) tail coefficient including the random earlier history, and the row-oversampling threshold for finite mean. Even arbitrarily small positive noise leaves square expected conditioning infinite; one extra ambient row restores a finite mean, materially distinguishing quantile safety from mean safety in a numerical linear algebra model.
